identification.title: As the Deer
identification.notes: Written 1981, published 1984 by Maranatha! Music. Verse 1 is Nystrom's setting of Psalm 42:1; verses 2 and 3 were added later by Lydia Pederson, which accounts for the shift in diction between them.

claims.structuralNotes: Three verses over one repeated chorus. Verse 1 paraphrases Psalm 42:1; verses 2 and 3 came later and from a different hand. Sung throughout in the first person singular, addressed directly to God.

claims.claim: The singer's longing for God is like a deer's thirst for water — need, not preference.
claims.subject: Longing for God
claims.lyricExcerpt: As the deer panteth for the water

claims.claim: God alone is the singer's strength and protection.
claims.subject: God as refuge
claims.lyricExcerpt: You alone are my strength, my shield

claims.claim: The singer yields their spirit to God alone.
claims.subject: Submission

claims.claim: God is worth more than gold, silver or any earthly good.
claims.subject: The worth of God

claims.claim: God is the giver of joy and the source of the singer's delight.
claims.subject: Joy in God

claims.claim: God is friend and brother to the singer, notwithstanding his kingship.
claims.subject: Christ's brotherhood
claims.lyricExcerpt: even though You are a King

claims.claim: God's love is worth more to the singer than any other love.
claims.subject: The love of God

strengths.title: Opens as a setting of Psalm 42
strengths.explanation: The first verse is the psalm's own image and its own longing, put in the congregation's mouth almost unaltered. The song's best line is not the songwriter's.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: As the deer panteth for the water
strengths.scriptureRationale: The psalm supplies both the thirst image and the object of the thirst.

strengths.title: God alone, named twice
strengths.explanation: The chorus makes God the exclusive object of trust and of submission. The repeated 'alone' is the doctrinal load-bearing word, and the congregation sings it every time.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: You alone are my strength, my shield
strengths.scriptureRationale: The psalm pairs strength and shield in the same confession of exclusive trust.

strengths.title: Desire is treated as worship
strengths.explanation: The song's whole action is wanting God, and it never resolves that wanting into a request for something else. Longing is left as its own act of worship.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The psalmist's desire for God above all else is presented as the fitting posture, not as an unmet need.

concerns.title: Brotherhood set against kingship
concerns.explanation: The concessive phrasing treats Christ's kingship as an obstacle his brotherhood overcomes. Hebrews grounds the brotherhood in his saving work, not in spite of his office — he is not our brother despite being King.
concerns.lyricExcerpt: even though You are a King
concerns.scriptureRationale: Christ is unashamed to call us brothers because he sanctifies us — the kingship is the ground, not the tension.

doctrinesAffirmed: God as the soul's true satisfaction
The worth of God above earthly good
theological.assessment: A short psalm-setting that does one thing and does it honestly. Its strength is that the best material is Scripture's own, and its chorus makes God the exclusive object of trust. The later verses are weaker than the first, and one line mishandles Christ's kingship, but nothing here is false. Sound for its purpose, and too narrow to carry a service by itself.

strengths.title: Learned in a single hearing
strengths.explanation: One short chorus, three short verses, no bridge and no key change. A congregation that has never met the song can sing the chorus the second time it comes round.

strengths.title: Nothing to negotiate
strengths.explanation: No syncopation to catch out untrained singers, no rhythmic hook that depends on a recording, and no held note at the climax. It survives a piano and a room.

concerns.title: Sung entirely in the singular
concerns.explanation: Every line is 'I' and 'my'. The congregation never says 'we', so a room of three hundred sings three hundred private songs at once. Not an error, but it shapes what the gathering is doing.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Sung here in A. That is a workable congregational key for this melody's shape, though churches commonly pitch it lower in G or F.

range.key: A (as sung here); widely published in C and D
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated. No publisher consulted lists a vocal range for the song.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The chorus repeats after every verse, but what repeats is the song's confession rather than a hook. Repetition here is doing the work it should.
communal.assessment: About as easy as a congregational song gets: short, stepwise, unhurried and indifferent to the band you have. The only communal weakness is that it never lets the congregation speak as one — it gives every singer a private first person and leaves them there.

strengths.title: One image, immediately understood
strengths.explanation: Thirst needs no explanation and no theological vocabulary. The song's central idea lands on a first hearing for a child and a stranger alike.

concerns.title: Two registers stitched together
concerns.explanation: The first verse keeps the psalm's older cadence; the verses added later speak in plain modern idiom. Sung end to end the seam shows, and the song sounds like two songs.

clarity.assessment: Plain and unambiguous throughout. Nothing in it can be misheard, and its one image carries the whole song. The only stylistic blemish is the join between the original verse and the two added later.

synthesis.summary: A simple setting of Psalm 42 whose chorus makes God the exclusive object of trust. Its best material is Scripture's own, and its weakest line makes Christ's kingship a tension rather than the ground of his brotherhood. Sound and easy to sing; too narrow in content to stand alone.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The source of the song's opening image and of its longing for the living God.
Pairs strength and shield in the same confession the chorus makes.
Grounds Christ's brotherhood in his saving work, which is what the third verse obscures.
